posts.title: Caffeine Detox Experiment
posts.text: Before the experiment 🧠 When it comes to having coffee, I would think of my experience in TikTok. When it was during the COVID-19 pandemic, I felt so depressed that I tried various ways to help me felt better because of getting quarantined at home. I got a cup of hand brewed pour-over coffee one day, and it was so fabulous. That's how my coffee dependency kicked off. Coffee did bring lots of happy experience to me. That said, coffee has also brought me troubles. For instance, I usually force myself to be awake through iced latte after burning the mid-night oil. I feel I am "awake", but actuall my brain has already broken down. How do I know that? Cuz I was like a "zombie", easy to forget things, hard to retrieve even simple info from memory. I'd say drinking coffee in a correct way would greatly improve life quality. I decided to try a caffeine detox experiment though. Just want to know if it helps. Experiment design Owning 0 experience about this field, I do some research online. And here’s a plan, I made it clearer by ChatGPT visualization. Here’s the 7-day plan of “Caffeine Detox Experiment”, I’d append my daily report below in next 7 days. Daily note 🤔 Day 1 Target: Cut down – Reduce usual intake Felt kind of happy and unhappy today. Feeling happy is because I’m making things different and trying something new to help me with my health. Feeling unhappy as I will lose some of my 🙃dopamine source. Maybe this is the last cup of coffee I will drink this week. Tomorrow, I will try with tea or a little bit instant coffee.By the way, simple coffee bean here is so simple in Auckland, at least in most of cafe. Maybe I didn’t get the correct way to be a coffee enthusiast here. I used to having special coffee beans in BeiJing, sometimes I have to admit that there are some benefits for “workforce advantage”🤣. Day 2 Target: Limit to half Got up early to go boat fishing, and drank a canned coffee to woke me up. Nothing chanllenging, nothing special. Just got seasick 🫠 Day 3 Target: No caffeine Do sleep well last night, I got up at near 8am today.Still half-asleep, I made myself a cup of coffee. Then pour it down the sink… Anyway, I felt a little bit dizzy and headache, but it’s okay. Day 4 Target: Experience the toughest day Realllllllly tough, even I had a good sleep last night, but during the day I felt a little bit dizzy and headache. Moveover, I couldn’t focus on anything. After 2 hours of struggle, I finally went into the flow. Meanwhile, I also found that it was vulnerable to get scrolling throught the screen when I couldn’t gather my mind. Just for reminder, keep phone away from me.🤛 Knocked out a few sets of back exercises, my head felt much better after that💪🏽 Day 5 Target: Energy improves Easily went to sleep last night, get up early today. I go for a walk outside and love soaking up the sun☀️. Even no other coffee, I can also be engergized. Day 6 Target: Reach a new balance I kind of feel nice today, without thinking about coffee or something that gives me dopamine. It’s like I were a flat person, being easy to satisfy and come into a state of flow.Free of distracting thoughts, the mind flows like a gentle, murmuring stream. Day 7 Target: Natural energy coming back! Beauuuuuuutiful day! Got up naturally even without alarm clock~ Full of energy all the day and have a car meetup with my friend.Less “cache miss”, more “cache hit” when retrieving information from memory. Conclusion🧑🏿‍💻 For me personally, I think the experiment works well. I felt much better after the experiment. I can also focus on my work more easily. That said, I won't give up drinking coffee or something with caffeine thoroughly, instead I would try to reduce the intake. After all, special coffee is fabulous.

posts.title: Phone Detox Experiment
posts.text: Before the experiment 🧠 Actually, getting lost scrolling through my phone has been a common thing for many of us, especially in a modern world, where we are always connected with others through social media. High tech IT companies hire top talents to design delicated algorithms, striving to stick users to their product, and then make profits. Don't be guilty for that, it's not our fault. That being said, we still ought to view this matter objectively. Internet grant us access to abundant information, yet we should not get trapped by cognitive overload. So, I decided to try a phone detox experiment, help me discover a world that I could talk more with myself. Experiment design As usual, here’s the 7-day plan of “Phone Detox Experiment”. I made this plan with ChatGPT based on my own experience. Hope I will follow the plan strictly🤣. Daily note 🤔 Day 1 Target: Awareness - How often I reach for devices? The day has just begun, I’m hoping to get off to great start💪. We’ll wait and see Conclusion🧑🏿‍💻

posts.title: Make a skill to help learning!
posts.text: Content123456789101112131415161718192021222324252627282930313233343536373839404142434445464748495051525354555657585960616263646566676869707172737475767778798081828384858687888990919293949596979899100101102103104105106107108109110---name: feynman-learningdescription: > Use this skill whenever the user wants to learn or deeply understand a concept using the Feynman technique. Trigger when the user says things like "teach me", "explain X to me", "I want to understand X", "help me learn X", "quiz me on X", "let's do Feynman on X", or "explain it like I'm a student". Also trigger when the user asks to test their own understanding of something they've just studied. The Feynman technique works by having the user explain the concept as if teaching it — Claude plays the student role, asking clarifying questions and using Socratic probing to surface gaps.---# Feynman Learning Skill## OverviewThis skill implements the Feynman Technique as an interactive learning session. The **user is the teacher**. Claude plays a **curious, genuine student** who is trying to understand the concept — not a quiz master, not an evaluator. Claude's job is to ask honest questions, expose gaps through Socratic dialogue, and help the user discover what they do and don't fully understand.---## The Feynman LoopThe session follows this cycle, repeating until the concept is solid:1. **Invite explanation** — Ask the user to explain the concept in their own words2. **Listen and track** — Note what's clear, what's vague, what's missing or contradictory3. **Probe with Socratic questions** — When something is unclear or incomplete, ask a genuine question (not "you got that wrong") to guide the user to discover the gap themselves4. **Reflect understanding back** — Occasionally paraphrase what you've understood to let the user verify or correct5. **Deepen or summarise** — Once a layer is solid, either push deeper or help the user crystallise a clean, simple summary---## Claude's Role: The StudentClaude should behave like a **smart but genuinely uninformed student**. This means:- Ask questions that a real learner would ask: "Wait, what does that actually mean?", "How is that different from X?", "Can you give me an example?"- Do **not** volunteer correct information or fill in gaps directly — ask a question that leads the user there instead- Do **not** evaluate or grade: avoid "Great explanation!" or "That's wrong." Stay in the student role- React naturally: if an explanation is confusing, say so. If something clicks, say so- **Never break character** to explain the concept yourself unless the user explicitly asks Claude to switch roles---## Calibrating to the User's LevelInfer the user's expertise from how they explain:| Signal | Adjust to ||---|---|| Uses precise technical terms correctly | Engage as a peer student, probe edge cases and nuance || Mix of correct and vague language | Engage as an intermediate learner, probe the vague parts || High-level or metaphor-heavy explanation | Engage as a beginner, ask "but how does that actually work?" |Do not ask the user what level they are — infer and adapt silently.---## Socratic Question PatternsWhen a gap or misconception appears, use questions like:- **Clarifying:** "When you say X, do you mean...? Or something else?"- **Concrete:** "Can you walk me through a specific example of that?"- **Edge case:** "What would happen if [boundary condition]? Would your explanation still hold?"- **Causal:** "Why does that happen? What causes it?"- **Contrast:** "How is that different from [related concept]?"- **Consequence:** "So if that's true, then [implication] — does that sound right?"Prefer one focused question at a time. Don't stack multiple questions.---## Session Structure### OpeningGreet the user as a student and invite them to start teaching:> "Sure! I'd love to understand [concept]. Can you start by explaining it to me like you're teaching someone who's never heard of it?"Adjust the framing if the user seems advanced — you might open as a student who "knows the basics" and wants to go deeper.### During the session- After each user response, either: - Ask a Socratic follow-up question (most common) - Paraphrase back your understanding and ask if it's correct - Ask for an example or analogy- Keep responses **short** — 1–3 sentences. The user should be doing most of the talking.### Wrapping upWhen the concept seems solid, offer to help the user crystallise a clean summary:> "Okay, I think I'm getting it. So, in simple terms: [your paraphrase of what the user explained]. Does that capture it?"This gives the user a chance to refine and own the final formulation.---## What to Avoid- **Don't explain the concept yourself** (unless the user explicitly asks to switch roles)- **Don't ask more than one question at a time**- **Don't praise or grade** — stay in the student role- **Don't pretend to be confused** about things that were clearly explained — only probe genuinely unclear or incomplete parts- **Don't rush to the summary** — the value is in the back-and-forth---## Switching RolesIf the user gets stuck and asks Claude to explain something, it's fine to briefly step out of the student role:> "Sure, I'll step out of student mode for a second. [Brief explanation.] Does that help? Want to pick back up from there?"Then return to the student role.

posts.title: The Silent Performance Killer - False Sharing in C++
posts.text: One day I ran into a weird performance issue when tunning the ring buffer module of a high performance C++ RPC framework. I cooperated with another colleague, aiming to write a fast ring buffer, somehow he updated the key struct definition, we weren’t on the same page though.Eventually the performance benchmark ended up performing poorly. In hindsight, the degradation was not directly a bug in the code, but a feature of the hardware. In our benchmark, the throughput under 2 threads was better than that of 8 threads, which was really interesting. That was caused by false sharing, one of the most counterintuitive performance bugs in concurrent C++. TL;DR False sharing occurs when multiple threads access and modify variables that reside on the same cache line, leading to a degradation in performance. False sharing can be avoided by using padding or alignment to separate variables on different cache lines. What’s False Sharing?False sharing happens when threads modify variables that happen to live on the same cache line. The variables themselves are unrelated, but the cache line keeps bouncing between cores, invalidated over and over, and that’s what kills the performance. Feynman Method Imagine you and a colleague are sharing a single whiteboard, but you each only need one small corner of it. You’re writing your notes in the top-left corner. Your colleague is writing theirs in the top-right corner. You never touch each other’s work. Completely independent. But here’s the catch: the whiteboard can only be erased and rewritten one person at a time. Every time you want to write something, you have to claim the whole whiteboard, which means your colleague has to stop, wait for you to finish, then reclaim it before they can write again. And vice versa. Neither of you is doing anything wrong. You’re not interfering with each other’s content at all. But you’re constantly blocking each other from using the board, because the rule operates on the whole whiteboard, not on individual corners. That whiteboard is a cache line. Your corner is variable x. Your colleague’s corner is variable y. The “claim the whole board” rule is the MESI coherence protocol. The fix is simple: get a second whiteboard. Put your notes on one, your colleague’s notes on the other. Now you never have to wait for each other. That’s what alignas does, it forces each variable onto its own cache line, its own whiteboard, so the two cores never have to fight over the same one. Start with an ExampleConsider the following code snippet: 12345678910111213141516171819202122232425262728293031323334353637383940414243444546474849505152#include <chrono>#include <cstdint>#include <iostream>#include <new>#include <thread>#include <vector>constexpr uint64_t kMaxTimes = 1000000000UL;#if 0 // X : bad examplestruct FalseSharing { volatile uint64_t x{0}; volatile uint64_t y{0};};#else// √ : good example, fixed the false-sharing issuestruct FalseSharing { alignas(64) volatile uint64_t x{0}; alignas(64) volatile uint64_t y{0};};#endifFalseSharing data;void WorkerA() { for (uint64_t i = 0; i < kMaxTimes; ++i) { ++data.x; }}void WorkerB() { for (uint64_t i = 0; i < kMaxTimes; ++i) { ++data.y; }}int main() { auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); std::thread t1(WorkerA); std::thread t2(WorkerB); t1.join(); t2.join(); auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); auto cost = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(end - start); std::cout << "Time cost totally: " << cost.count() << " ms \n";} Building and running this gives: When false-sharing: When fixed: The performance result gap is significant, it costs 1776 ms to run the code snippet with false-sharing, while 409 ms to run it with fixed false-sharing issue.And it will be even worse if we run it on more cores. When reproducing the case by yourself, it should be noted that: We should compile with -O3, otherwise the compiler will optimize away the false-sharing issue. Sepecifically, it will simply remove the loop and add the final result. It was like “You nerd, why not add the variable all at once??”. We should use volatile to ensure that the compiler doesn’t optimize away the access to the variables in the example. Otherwise, the variable is cached in the CPU register, making it hard to observe the performance degradation. Since it optimizes away a ton of DRAM memory access. Under the HoodCPUs don’t read individual bytes from RAM. They read in fixed-size chunks called cache lines, typically 64 bytes on most modern x86 and ARM processors. When a core accesses any byte in memory, the entire 64-byte line containing it is pulled into L1 cache. This is usually a win. But in multithreaded code, it creates a trap. Suppose Thread A writes to x and Thread B writes to y. Different variables, different threads, no logical sharing. But if x and y sit within the same 64-byte cache line, the CPU doesn’t know that. Every time Thread A writes, it acquires exclusive ownership of the line, which invalidates Thread B’s copy. Thread B then reloads the line before it can write. Then A’s copy is invalidated. Back and forth, millions of times per second. This is false sharing: threads that don’t share data logically, but are forced by hardware to behave as if they do. The mechanism is the MESI cache coherence protocol. A write transitions a cache line to Modified on the writing core and broadcasts Invalid to all other cores holding a copy. Each invalidation costs dozens to hundreds of cycles and they never stop. SolutionMethod1: PaddingBy adding padding to the struct, we can separate the variables onto different cache lines, which avoids false sharing. In C++, we can use keyword alignas to align the variables. 123456// √ : good example, fixed the false-sharing issue// Usually 64 byte cache line, in C++17 `alignas(std::hardware_destructive_interference_size)` is the right answer.struct FixFalseSharing { alignas(64) volatile uint64_t x{0}; alignas(64) volatile uint64_t y{0};}; The padding happens during compilation phase by adding padding bit between the variables. Method2: Thread localAnother way to avoid false sharing is to use thread-local storage by rethinking the design if possible.By declaring the variables as thread-local, each thread gets its own copy of the variable, which avoids false sharing.It’s like: 1thread_local uint64_t x; // each process has its own version Caveats Padding wastes memory. A padded char occupies 64 bytes instead of 1, and for a large array of padded structs, that 8x memory bloat can hurt cache efficiency at a higher level than the false sharing you were fixing. 64 bytes is the common cache line size on x86/ARM today, but it isn’t universal. Prefer std::hardware_destructive_interference_size over hardcoding the number. True sharing is a different problem. If two threads genuinely need to access the same variable, padding does nothing, that’s a synchronisation problem, not a layout problem. To confirm false sharing is actually the cause, run perf stat -e cache-misses ./xxxx on Linux. A suspiciously high cache miss rate under the parallel workload is usually the tell. False sharing happens at every cache level, but it hurts worst at L1. Each core’s L1 and L2 are private, so when two cores write to variables on the same cache line, the coherence protocol keeps invalidating those private copies. The reloading core usually finds a valid copy in the shared L3 (about 40 cycles) instead of going all the way to RAM, since the contested line stays hot in the hierarchy from the other core’s writes. The cost isn’t the fetch distance, it’s how often the invalidation happens: a 4-cycle L1 hit turns into a 40-cycle L3 reload on every single write. Across NUMA sockets with no shared L3, it gets worse still. Key takeaway

posts.title: Reflection - System Design Process
posts.text: For a long time I sat on the other side of the table. I interviewed a lot of candidates on system design, and the pattern was consistent: the ones who struggled had no frame to hang the problem on. They’d dive straight into databases or microservices and then get lost. The ones who did well slowed down and worked through the problem in an order that made sense. I ended up on the interviewee side recently, and I wanted a process I could actually follow. The infographic is what I landed on. Six phases, roughly 10 minutes each, totalling about an hour. 👔Step 1: business use cases (10 min)Before any technical decision, understand the problem. Who are the users? What are they actually trying to do? What does “working” look like? This is the easiest step to skip and the hardest to recover from. If you get the use cases wrong, you’ll end up with something architecturally coherent that solves the wrong problem. Interviewers notice when candidates jump straight to components. The ones who do well ask questions first. 🦾Step 2: constraints (10 min)Once you know what, figure out how much. What’s the expected QPS? What latency does the use case actually need? How much data? What’s the availability target? Don’t skip budget, timeline, or compliance. Real systems have real limits. Stating constraints explicitly gives you something to point back to when you make trade-offs later. 🏰Step 3: architecture (10 min)Now draw the high-level picture. What are the major components? Where are the boundaries? What technology are you choosing, and why? Walk through the data flow. This doesn’t need to be a final production design. It needs to be a coherent skeleton that can hold up to questions. Show that you can decompose a complex system into parts someone else can follow. ⌨️Step 4: API design (10 min)With the architecture sketched, define the contracts between components. What are the key endpoints? What do requests and responses look like? How do you handle auth, errors, versioning? Candidates often get vague here. Interviewers who’ve worked in production know that badly designed APIs cause pain for years. Be specific. 📊Step 5: database choice (10 min)Pick the right storage layer, and explain why. SQL or NoSQL depends on your data model, access patterns, and consistency requirements. Talk about sharding, indexing, caching, failure handling. The point isn’t to always reach for the same tool. It’s to show you can reason about trade-offs: read-heavy vs write-heavy, strong vs eventual consistency. Rattling off database names without that reasoning doesn’t go far. 📀Step 6: data model (10 min)Finally, get concrete about the data. Define your entities and their relationships. Specify primary keys and indexes. Think about what happens to the schema at scale. A well-thought-out data model often exposes assumptions from earlier steps that don’t hold up. That’s a good sign. Going back and revising shows you’re thinking through the problem, not filling out a template. Wrapping up Keep it simple, communicate clearly, iterate and refine. That’s mostly it. The interview isn’t asking whether you know every database or can sketch the perfect architecture in 10 minutes. It’s asking whether you can navigate an open-ended problem without losing the thread. The six steps are a scaffold, not a script. Practice it enough that it becomes automatic. Then the mental energy you’re not spending on process can go toward the parts of the problem that are actually hard.

posts.title: What's true understanding?
posts.text: Recently I’ve taken a class in UoA called “Self-Leadership”, which has given me a great deal of food for thought. It was somewhat novel and unfamiliar to me, and I mistook it for a typical self-success course.But the course content turned out to be surprisingly insightful. I’ve learned the most fundamental practice of self-leadership: reflection. There is no secret formula or magic behind it. It simply offers me a quiet chance to pause, slow down, and reflect on my inner self. TL;DR The illusion of understanding is a common trap in learning, where we feel like we understand something but lack genuine mastery. Use Feynman’s Method to check if you understand the concept. ObservationThese days I spent plenty of time diving into CSAPP, a classic book in computer science. Over the past few years in my work, I always intended to read this book thoroughly, but never got around to it. What I found interesting is that I acted differently. I somehow took on two distinct approaches once I began learning basic concepts such as Virtual Memory and Set Associative Caches. To summarize, I understand Set Associative Caches better than Virtual Memory. Meanwhile, reading the chapter on Virtual Memory felt more enjoyable and rewarding. In contrast, studying the other topic is quite challenging and “full of dopamine”. InflectionWhy?It is an issue with the illusion of understanding. It is recognition, yet not genuine mastery. When I closed the book, and looked back at the whole picture of Virtual Memory. I asked myself, but I got stuck over and over again. I couldn’t clarify the details of the concept, and I came up with some new questions. It ended up the knowledge is like a cyclone, it comes and goes, leaving a mess. I think the reason is that I used to use Virtual Memory a lot in my work. Therefore, I just read the concepts happily without stop thinking more about it. There was a voice in mind said “Yeah, that’s it. The layout is just like that. The underlying mechanism is just like that.”. I was so satisfied that I had learnt so much again. (Maybe after several days, I could be “happy” once more). 😔 In terms of Set Associative Caches, it’s not a huge knowledge, so I break it down into smaller parts and draw diagrams to help me understand it better. I somehow map the diagrams in my mind, and start explaining it to myself. Every time I get stuck by something that I can’t make it clear, I just go back to the book and read it again. Eventually, I really master it! I can spot connections between it and my existing knowledge. 😁 Implication && ActionI may have tried these methods consciously or unconsciously before. But now I need to define them clearly and supervise myself to see if I can put them into practice 👊. Thinking about how to articulate the ideas without opening the book. Actually it’s Feynman’s Method. Personally, I can understand about 90% of new knowledge after using the Feynman Method. Drawing diagrams to help me understand the concepts better. Break down the knowledge into smaller parts, making it easier to take action. AttachmentHere’s the Pros. and Cons. of using Feynman’s Method, just for you information.
